content: 1. The preferred non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) for antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens in patients receiving rifampicin-based antibiotic treatment for Buruli ulcer (BU) is efavirenz. If efavirenz is unavailable, nevirapine can be used, but a lead-in dose of nevirapine is not required when rifampicin is part of the treatment regimen. 2. Caution is advised when using nevirapine-containing regimens, particularly in patients with high or unknown CD4 cell counts at ART initiation, due to an increased risk of hypersensitivity reactions and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Close monitoring during the initial weeks of therapy is recommended for these patients. 3. If efavirenz cannot be used, integrase inhibitors such as raltegravir may be considered as an alternative to nevirapine, if available. 4. Protease inhibitors (PIs) should be avoided during BU antibiotic treatment with rifampicin, as rifampicin significantly reduces PI levels. If a patient is already on a PI-based regimen, and they are NNRTI-naïve and not infected with HIV-2, the PI should be replaced with an NNRTI-based regimen using efavirenz. 5. The use of tenofovir (TDF) in patients receiving streptomycin as part of BU treatment may increase the risk of renal toxicity. Renal function should be closely monitored, and additional factors that may impair renal function should be avoided. 6. Efavirenz is no longer contraindicated during the first trimester of pregnancy. 7. All children under the age of 5 years should initiate ART within 8 weeks of starting BU treatment. For children aged 5 years and older, the timing of ART initiation should follow the same recommendations as for adults. 8. Efavirenz is not approved for use in children under 3 years of age. In this age group, if ART is initiated during BU treatment with rifampicin, nevirapine should be used at a dose of 200 mg/m², or alternatively, a triple NRTI regimen (e.g., AZT/3TC/ABC or AZT/3TC/TDF) can be considered. 9. If a child is already on a PI-based ART regimen when starting BU treatment with rifampicin, the dose of ritonavir (RTV) should be increased to achieve a 1:1 ratio with lopinavir (LPV). Alternatively, the LPV/RTV regimen can be replaced with nevirapine at a dose of 200 mg/m² or a triple NRTI regimen. Integrase inhibitors such as raltegravir may also be considered as a replacement for the PI, if available and appropriate. 10. For patients known to be HIV-positive or screened as HIV-positive at the initiation of BU treatment, ART should be started as soon as possible within 8 weeks of starting BU treatment if the CD4 count is ≤500 cells/mm³ or if the patient has WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 HIV disease. Priority should be given to those with advanced HIV disease (CD4 <350 cells/mm³ or WHO stage 3 or 4 disease). 11. For patients with CD4 counts >500 cells/mm³, ART should not be initiated until the CD4 count falls to ≤500 cells/mm³ or other criteria for ART initiation are met. If CD4 testing is unavailable, ART should be started within 8 weeks of BU treatment initiation for patients with WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 HIV disease. 12. Patients already receiving ART at the time of BU diagnosis should continue their ART regimen. If the regimen includes nevirapine, it should be replaced with efavirenz if there are no contraindications. If efavirenz is unavailable, nevirapine can be continued. 13. If a patient is on a PI-based regimen, and they are NNRTI-naïve and not infected with HIV-2, the PI should be replaced with an NNRTI-based regimen using efavirenz. If this is not possible, adjusted-dose PI regimens (e.g., double-dose LPV/RTV or standard LPV with adjusted RTV doses) can be used, but these regimens are associated with high toxicity and require close clinical and laboratory monitoring. 14. If a patient is taking TDF and streptomycin is part of the BU treatment regimen, renal function should be closely monitored, and factors that may impair renal function should be avoided. 15. HIV testing is recommended for all BU patients because BU may be more common in HIV-infected individuals, and HIV coinfection can significantly impact BU management and treatment outcomes. Determining the HIV status of the patient is essential for optimizing BU care. 16. ART initiation should be explained to patients, particularly those with CD4 counts ≤500 cells/mm³, as delays in ART initiation may increase HIV-associated morbidity and mortality. Early ART initiation may also improve BU treatment outcomes by enhancing immune function. 17. For patients with CD4 counts >500 cells/mm³, the risks of early ART initiation, such as increased side effects, pill burden, and potential drug interactions, may outweigh the benefits. WHO guidelines do not recommend ART in this group unless they have advanced HIV disease, TB or HBV coinfection, or are in a serodiscordant relationship. 18. Research is urgently needed to better understand the epidemiological, clinical, and treatment implications of BU-HIV coinfection. This includes studying the burden of BU in HIV-infected patients, the impact of HIV on BU disease severity and treatment outcomes, and the optimal timing and safety of ART during BU treatment.
